A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same positional-attention architecture and retain matching numeric experiments. Their main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial expansion.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C report original training and generalization experiments on five numeric algorithmic tasks, including sample-size, input-length, and architecture comparisons.

after.justification: Section 7 and Appendix D retain numeric experiments and report additional original results on induction heads, mixed textual/numeric inputs, architectural ablations, and additional baselines.

M1.justification: The core layer and positional-only attention equations remain unchanged. Appendices D.2–D.3 introduce limited task-specific adaptations: causal masking and token-output logits for induction heads, and separate token embeddings and numeric projections for mixed inputs.

E1.justification: The five numeric tasks and fixed/variable-length coverage are retained. v2 adds k-hop induction heads with unseen-symbol testing and mixed textual/numeric conditional aggregation with unseen categories and changed distractor patterns. Appendix D.1.9 also evaluates integer inputs for rounding-based accuracy.

E2.justification: v2 retains standard Transformer, compact-model, and RoPE comparisons while adding GCN and GAT on cumulative sum and sorting using complete/star graphs (Table 1). It also adds fine-tuned GPT2-large comparisons on mixed-input tasks (Figure 34), substantially expanding the comparator families.

E3.justification: The reported numeric-task learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 5e-4; the PDFs do not establish reruns. New protocols include length-30 induction heads with at most three hops and cross-entropy evaluation, rounding/tolerance-based whole-list accuracy, and GPT2 MSE/MAPE scoring that excludes unparseable outputs (Appendix D).

E4.justification: Beyond retained compact-model, RoPE, and attention-map analyses, v2 adds binary/sinusoidal encoding tests and seven architectural configurations examining input representation and positional-encoding placement (D.1.6–D.1.7). New depth and sample-size analyses investigate induction-head failures and mixed-input generalization (D.2–D.3).

E5.justification: Both versions report medians over ten runs with 10th–90th percentile bands. v2 extends this practice to additional plots, including Figure 34, without reporting a changed run count, seed policy, or uncertainty-estimation method.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial findings: standard Transformers achieve near-zero induction-head in-distribution loss with three layers, while positional Transformers perform worse and both generalize poorly to unseen symbols (Figures 3 and 5). Mixed-input, GNN, encoding, ablation, accuracy, and GPT2 results are also newly reported. These additions are distinct from retained numeric curves.

T1.justification: v1's PCOC simulation theorem is retained as Lemma B.2. v2 adds MPC simulation with logarithmic depth overhead, simulation of standard Transformers, and accompanying routing constructions and proofs (Theorem 5.1, Remark 5.1, Appendix B). Theorem 6.1 and Appendix C introduce a norm-based generalization bound with covering-number and Rademacher-complexity analysis.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds an average 1000-fold OOD improvement and PCOC expressivity. v2 redefines the contributions around MPC expressivity, in-distribution learnability, and task-dependent OOD performance. Its abstract and introduction explicitly acknowledge learning tradeoffs and poor induction-head generalization, narrowing the practical superiority claim.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a depth-versus-parameter-norm tradeoff in sample complexity and hypothesizes that dynamic communication makes induction-head optimization difficult. New ablations support interpretations about positional-encoding placement. Section 7.3 also explicitly cautions that mixed-input results do not establish superiority on general-purpose textual reasoning.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproduction information, including token/numeric encoding instructions, mixed-task batch size 1024, and GPT2 digit formatting, BPE tokenization, and fine-tuning on 50,000 samples for three epochs. However, v1's explicit experiment-code link is absent from v2; this establishes removed access information, not repository unavailability.

R1.justification: v1 motivates PCOC partly through its differences from Sanford et al.'s MPC approach. v2 positions PCOC as a bridge to MPC and standard Transformers, and adds substantive engagement with norm-based learning theory through Edelman et al. and Bartlett–Mendelson. Beneš networks, induction-head work, GPT2, and newer algorithmic-reasoning studies add further research connections.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. PCOC definitions move into Appendix A, learnability becomes a main section, and experiments are reorganized from fixed/variable-length regimes into in-distribution, OOD, and mixed-input sections. The appendix structure is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds a Beneš-network diagram, the GNN results table, and numerous induction-head, mixed-input, ablation, and accuracy plots. Existing figures are redistributed or reformatted: v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 19, existing in-distribution panels receive main-text prominence, and appendix charts adopt shared legends and explicit in-distribution/OOD labels.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper through the MPC connection and explicit learnability analysis, while new ablations and negative induction-head results better establish the mechanism's applicability boundaries than v1's broad advantage claim. These gains outweigh reporting drawbacks: the explicit code link disappears, and Appendix D.3 inconsistently names a mixed-input variant as max while Figures 6, 32, and 34 label it sum. Those issues limit reproducibility but do not erase the substantial theoretical and evidential gains.
